paper_a.title: Exact Matrix Completion via Convex Optimization

metadata.description: Both papers solve the low-rank matrix completion problem from a uniformly random subset of entries, but via fundamentally different theoretical frameworks. Candes-Recht use convex optimization (nuclear-norm minimization, an SDP) and analyze it through duality and a dual-certificate construction; Keshavan-Montanari-Oh (OptSpace) use a non-convex three-step algorithm (trim, rank-r SVD projection, gradient descent on a Grassmann manifold) and analyze it through manifold optimization and singular-value perturbation. The two are also explicitly compared in paper B's Section 1.6 (Candes-Plan SDP error bound is cited as a benchmark). This is a textbook competing-frameworks pair: same problem, same incoherence-style assumptions, different machinery, different guarantees (exact recovery in the noiseless setting for paper A; Frobenius error bounds under noise for paper B).

matches.explanation: Both papers state the central matrix completion problem: recover a low-rank matrix from a random subset of its entries. Paper A states it as exact recovery from $m \ll n_1 n_2$ entries; paper B states the noisy version (recover M from N=M+Z observed on E) but the underlying problem object is the same. The noisy/exact distinction surfaces in the theorems, not in the problem statement.

Paper A's optimization formulations are convex: rank minimization (NP-hard) and its nuclear-norm relaxation (an SDP). Paper B's optimization formulation is non-convex: minimize the regularized cost $\tilde F(X,Y)$ over the Grassmann product manifold. Both are the algorithmic targets of their respective papers but they live in completely different optimization landscapes (convex vs non-convex Riemannian).

The generalized low-rank recovery from arbitrary linear measurements (Candes-Recht's extension to inner-product measurements with bases f_i, g_j) has no counterpart in paper B, which restricts attention to the entrywise sampling operator throughout.

Both papers define the entrywise sampling operator (Paper A: $P_\Omega$ / $\mathcal{R}_\Omega$; Paper B: $\mathcal{P}_E$). Identical mathematical object: orthogonal projection onto the observed-index subspace, $0$ elsewhere.

Both papers introduce incoherence conditions controlling how aligned the singular vectors of M are with the standard basis. Paper A uses subspace coherence $\mu(U) = (n/r) \max_i \|P_U e_i\|^2$ with two assumptions (A0: subspace coherence bounded; A1: sign-matrix entrywise bound). Paper B's $(\mu_0,\mu_1)$-incoherence is essentially the same two conditions (A1 in B = A0 in A; A2 in B = A1 in A) phrased directly on rows of U,V. The match is exact at the level of role and quantitative content; the names $\mu_0, \mu_1$ even agree across papers.

Paper A's tangent space $T$ (linear span of matrices $u_k x^*, y v_k^*$ at the truth) and paper B's product Grassmann manifold $\mathcal{M}(m,n) = G(m,r) \times G(n,r)$ both encode the local geometry of rank-$r$ matrices around the truth. They play analogous roles - paper A uses $T$ as a linear-subspace device for the dual certificate, paper B uses $\mathcal{M}$ as the actual nonlinear manifold over which gradient descent runs. The objects are related (T is the tangent space at the truth to the smooth rank-r manifold) but used very differently: T is a linear projection target in A, M(m,n) is the optimization domain in B.

The 'random orthogonal model' (M with uniformly random singular vectors) is paper A's specialised low-rank model used for Theorem 1.1; paper B does not use a random model for M, instead working under deterministic incoherence.
The 'incoherent basis model' with random sign sequence is paper A's secondary random model; paper B has no analogue.
The subgradient characterisation of the nuclear norm is core to paper A's duality-based analysis; paper B avoids the nuclear norm entirely (it is mentioned only via the cited identity EP104.1).
Paper A explicitly switches between uniform and Bernoulli sampling (with a reduction RP103.3); paper B works with the uniform model throughout.

Paper A defines the nuclear norm $\|X\|_* = \sum_k \sigma_k(X)$ as a paper-original definition (the paper's central object). Paper B mentions the nuclear-norm factor identity $\|M\|_* = \frac{1}{2}\min_{M=XY^T}\{\|X\|_F^2 + \|Y\|_F^2\}$ (citing Srebro-Rennie-Jaakkola/Recht-Fazel-Parrilo) only as motivation for its alternative manifold approach. Same underlying object, used as foreground vs cited prior work.
Paper A introduces Schatten q-norms (used in noncommutative Khintchine arguments); paper B's analysis uses operator and Frobenius norms only.
Paper B's noisy observation model $N = M + Z$ with revealed entries on E has no counterpart in paper A, which treats the noiseless exact-recovery problem.

The average sampling rate $\epsilon = |E|/\sqrt{mn}$ is a paper-B normalisation; paper A uses $p = m/(n_1 n_2)$ (Bernoulli probability) which is closely related but plays a different role in its analysis.

Trimming (zero out high-degree rows/columns of $N^E$) is a uniquely Keshavan-Montanari-Oh contribution; absent from paper A which has no need for it because the SDP analysis goes via the full $P_\Omega$ operator.
Rank-r projection $\mathcal{T}_r$ (rescaled best rank-r SVD approximation) is the second step of OptSpace. Paper A does not use rank truncation as part of its algorithm.

Paper B's cost function $F(X,Y) = \min_S \frac12 \sum_{(i,j)\in E}(N_{ij}-(XSY^T)_{ij})^2$ and its regularised variant $\tilde F$ are paper-B-specific non-convex objectives; paper A minimises the nuclear norm instead.

Grassmann distance $d(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2)$, auxiliary distances $d_-,d_+$, and bounded-row constraint set $\mathcal{C}(\mu)$ are all internal devices of the OptSpace convergence analysis on the manifold; no analogue in paper A.

Paper B's noise models (sub-Gaussian iid entries; bounded worst-case) are necessary because paper B treats noisy observations. Paper A is noiseless and has no noise assumption (although OpenP103.3 raises the noisy case as an open problem).

Both are matrix-completion algorithms with the same input/output signature (sparse observations, target rank/structure $\to$ recovered matrix), but the algorithms themselves are completely different. Paper A: nuclear-norm SDP solved by interior-point method. Paper B: trim + rank-r SVD + Grassmann gradient descent (OptSpace). This is the core algorithmic axis of the competing-frameworks relationship.
PSD trace minimisation (the symmetric variant of the nuclear-norm SDP) is a paper-A-specific specialisation of the convex method to PSD inputs.

Both papers' main recovery theorems quantify when the algorithm succeeds in terms of (sample size $m$ or $|E|$, rank $r$, incoherence $\mu_0,\mu_1$, dimension $n$). Paper A: $m \ge C \mu_0 n^{6/5} r \log n$ implies exact recovery of M with high probability. Paper B (Thm 1.2): $|E| \ge C n \sqrt{\alpha} \kappa^2 \max(\mu_0 r \sqrt\alpha \log n, \mu_0^2 r^2 \alpha \kappa^4, \mu_1^2 r^2 \alpha \kappa^4)$ implies $\frac{1}{\sqrt{mn}}\|\hat M - M\|_F \le C' \kappa^2 (n\sqrt{r\alpha}/|E|) \|Z^E\|_2$. They differ fundamentally in conclusion: A guarantees exact recovery (noiseless), B guarantees a Frobenius error bound proportional to the noise level. The sample-complexity scaling in r is also different (A has linear in $r$ up to logs; B has $r^2$ at leading order outside the small-$r$ regime). Same role (main performance guarantee), substantially different statements.
Theorem 1.1 (Trim+SVD error bound) is the noisy spectral guarantee for the second step of OptSpace; paper A has no spectral / SVD-based intermediate result because it does not use SVD truncation.
Operator-norm bounds on $\tilde Z^E$ under sub-Gaussian and worst-case noise are paper-B-specific; paper A is noiseless so does not need these bounds.

The Rudelson-type near-isometry $\|P_T P_\Omega P_T - p P_T\| \lesssim \sqrt{\mu_0 nr \log n / m}$ is the central operator-concentration ingredient in the dual-certificate construction. Paper B avoids this entirely - its analysis runs through Grassmann optimisation, not through restricted isometry on T.
Bernoulli deviation bound on $P_\Omega - p I$ (paper-A-original spectral concentration) has no counterpart in paper B's analysis.

Lemmas 'incoherent bases satisfy A1' and 'random orthogonal coherence' are paper-A internal results connecting the two random models to the deterministic incoherence assumptions. Paper B never assumes a random model.

Uniqueness via dual certificate is the cornerstone of the convex-optimization analysis (paper A). Paper B's manifold-gradient-descent analysis has no dual certificate; uniqueness of the global optimum is not even claimed (only convergence to a local stationary point near the truth).

The order-0 through order-3 spectral bounds plus the high-order tail are the technical machinery of paper A's dual-certificate construction (controlling each term of the Neumann series for $(P_T P_\Omega P_T)^{-1}$). Paper B has no analogous power-series device.

Auxiliary lemmas in paper A's spectral-bound chain (Bernstein on Q(X), diagonal-sandwich, off-diagonal, $\nu(\mathcal{H}^3(E))$, row-sum, Bernstein on $\sum \delta E^2$, $H_\omega$ bound). All paper-A-internal.
Bound on $\|P_\Omega P_T\|$ is a paper-A corollary of TP103.3; no counterpart in paper B.

Paper B's chain of auxiliary lemmas: singular-value perturbation of $\tilde N^E$, quadratic bounds on $F$, gradient lower bound, noiseless quadratic, noiseless gradient, directional gradient, control of $S - \Sigma$. All paper-B-internal manifold-analysis machinery with no convex-optimisation analogue.
Nuclear-spectral duality (cited from Recht 2007) is an external paper-A ingredient; paper B does not invoke it. Both are origin=external so this does not influence the relation_type.

Cited results from KMO 2009 (spectral-norm bound on $M - (\sqrt{mn}/\epsilon) \tilde M^E$; distance-Frobenius bound) are paper-B-internal external citations to a precursor work. Paper A does not cite these.

Cited results: Seginer's expected operator norm bound and Talagrand concentration. Paper A also uses Talagrand concentration (LP103.20), but the citation in paper A and paper B serve different sub-arguments and are origin=external so no informative cross-paper match. Do not emit external-vs-external matches that don't shape the pair-level relation.

Both papers cite the same Talagrand 1996 concentration result. This is an external-vs-external coincidence, both serving the role of concentrating an operator-norm-like supremum around its mean. Carries no information about the A-B relationship (per the prompt's guidance on external matches), but emitted because the cited theorem is the same.
Chi-squared concentration (Laurent-Massart) is cited only by paper A in service of its random-orthogonal-model analysis.
Noncommutative Khintchine, decoupling, and Hadamard-product spectral bounds are paper-A-only external lemmas (Lust-Picquard, de la Pena-Gine, Ando-Horn-Johnson) supporting the spectral-bound chain.

Paper A's sample-size threshold equation $m \ge C \max(\mu_1^2, \mu_0^{1/2}\mu_1, \mu_0 n^{1/4}) nr (\beta \log n)$ is the precise condition under which the SDP recovers M. The corresponding object in paper B is the sample-size hypothesis inside Theorem 1.2 (TP104.2). Both express 'how many samples suffice' for their respective methods; the scalings are not equal but they play the same role.
Power-series inversion $(P_T P_\Omega P_T)^{-1} = p^{-1}(I + \mathcal{H} + \mathcal{H}^2 + \ldots)$ is the algebraic backbone of paper A's dual certificate via Neumann series; absent from paper B.
The dual-certificate ansatz $Y = R^*_\Omega (R^*_\Omega R_\Omega)^{-1}(E)$ (the minimum-Frobenius-norm dual matrix) is paper A's central construction; paper B has no dual certificate.

Paper B's section 1.6 cites the Candes-Plan SDP error bound and the oracle MMSE bound to compare OptSpace with nuclear-norm minimisation. These are origin=external in paper B (citing Candes-Plan 2010), so do not match against any concrete node in paper A's graph (which is the 2009 noiseless paper, not Candes-Plan 2010). Notable that this is the explicit comparison-with-other-approaches anchor.
Worst-case operator-norm lower bound illustrating necessity of trimming is paper-B-specific.
Coupon-collector lower bound on sample complexity is paper-A's discussion of optimality of the log factor. Paper B does not state an analogous lower bound.
Bipartite-graph connectivity argument for impossibility of recovery from disconnected sample patterns is paper-A-specific.
Bernoulli vs uniform reduction is paper A's bookkeeping device for switching between sampling models.
Rescaling-into-$\mathcal{C}(3\mu_0)$ remark is internal bookkeeping for OptSpace's convergence analysis on the manifold.
Paper A poses the open problem of optimal $nr \log n$ sample complexity; paper B does not pose this as an open problem (and, separately, OptSpace's bound has a similar gap).
Approximate recovery for approximately-low-rank matrices is paper A's open problem.

Paper A explicitly raises noisy matrix completion as an open problem (OpenP103.3): can constrained nuclear-norm SDP achieve recovery error proportional to noise level? Paper B's main theorem TP104.2 is precisely a positive answer for the OptSpace algorithm (not for nuclear-norm SDP), giving an error bound $\propto \|Z^E\|_2$. So paper B answers paper A's open problem in the noisy regime, but with a different algorithm. This is a strong signal for the competing-frameworks relation: same question, two solution paths.
Proof of uniqueness via dual certificate (paper A's central proof). No analogue in paper B.
Proof of Rudelson-type near-isometry (paper A's central operator-concentration proof).

Both proofs establish their main recovery theorem, but via radically different routes. Paper A's PP103.3 combines five spectral-bound lemmas (orders 0,1,2,3 plus high-order tail) on a Neumann-series expansion of the dual certificate, then invokes the uniqueness lemma. Paper B's PP104.3 combines quadratic bounds (LP104.3), the corollary on $S-\Sigma$, and the gradient lower bound (LP104.4) to show iterates stay in $\mathcal{C}(4\mu_0)$ and converge to a stationary point near the truth. Same role (proof of main theorem), entirely different machinery.
Paper A's auxiliary proofs (random-orthogonal coherence, order-0, order-1, order-2, order-3, high-order, incoherent-bases). All internal to the dual-certificate spectral-bound chain.

Paper B's auxiliary proofs (singular-value perturbation, Theorem 1.1, Lemma 2.1 quadratic, Corollary 2.2, Lemma 2.3 gradient, Theorem 1.3 independent and worst-case). All internal to the manifold-optimisation analysis.

Both papers run phase-transition / RMSE numerical experiments on synthetic random low-rank matrices to validate the theory. Paper A: phase-transition curves on $40\times 40$ and $50\times 50$ matrices for full and PSD cases. Paper B: directly compares OptSpace against nuclear-norm minimisation (i.e., paper A's method) on rank-2 $600\times 600$ matrices, plotting RMSE versus $|E|$. Paper B's experiment is in fact a direct head-to-head with paper A, reinforcing the competing-frameworks narrative.
Recovery from Gaussian projections, the rank-1 $e_1 e_n^*$ counterexample motivating incoherence, and multitask-learning application are paper-A-only examples.
OptSpace convergence experiment at $|E|/n=80,160$ and the all-ones matrix illustrating necessity of trimming are paper-B-specific.
